# Introduction

Nestimate (Saqr, López-Pernas, & Misiejuk, 2026) estimates networks from
sequence and panel data, and cograph draws them. The two packages divide
the work: Nestimate computes the networks, their resampling, comparisons
and clusterings, and returns objects that cograph's `splot()` draws
directly. This tutorial follows one dataset through the steps of a
transition network analysis (Saqr et al., 2025; Saqr, López-Pernas, &
Tikka, 2025), which has been used, for example, to map students'
self-regulated learning tactics (Peeters, Saqr, & Viberg, 2020):
estimating the network, checking the stability of its edges
and centralities, comparing groups, and grouping the states into clusters.

| Step | Nestimate | cograph |
|------|-----------|---------|
| Estimate a network | `build_network()` | `splot()` |
| Stability of the edges | `bootstrap_network()` | `splot()`, `plot_bootstrap_forest()` |
| Stability of the centralities | `centrality_stability()` | `splot()` |
| Networks per group | `build_network(group = )` | `splot()` |
| Compare groups | `permutation()` | `splot()` |
| Clusters of states | `build_mcml()`, `as_tna()` | `splot()` |

# Data

`group_regulation_long` records the regulation actions of students
working in groups, one row per action, with the student (`Actor`), the
time (`Time`) and the action (`Action`). It is generated synthetically
from the `group_regulation` dataset of the tna package (Tikka,
López-Pernas, & Saqr, 2025). The nine actions, `adapt`, `cohesion`,
`consensus`, `coregulate`, `discuss`, `emotion`, `monitor`, `plan` and
`synthesis`, are the nodes of the networks below. `Achiever` marks each
student as a high or a low achiever.

```{r}
library(Nestimate)
library(cograph)
head(group_regulation_long)
```

# Estimating networks

## A transition network

`build_network()` estimates a network from the data. With
`method = "relative"`, the weight of the edge from one action to another is
the probability that the second follows the first, so each row of the
weight matrix sums to 1.

```{r}
net <- build_network(group_regulation_long, action = "Action",
                     actor = "Actor", time = "Time", method = "relative")
net
extract_initial_probs(net)
```

The strongest transitions lead to `consensus`: from `cohesion` (0.50),
from `adapt` (0.48) and from `synthesis` (0.47). `consensus` is also the
most frequent first action (0.21), followed by `plan` (0.20). The network
is a `netobject`, which inherits from `cograph_network`, so `splot()`
draws it.

```{r}
splot(net)
```

## Other estimators

`method` selects the estimator; `list_estimators()` lists them.

```{r}
list_estimators()
```

Fifteen estimators are available. The directed ones (`relative`,
`frequency`, `attention`, `ngram`, `gap`, `reverse`, `latency`, `wtna`)
describe which action follows which; the undirected ones (`cor`, `pcor`,
`glasso`, `ising`, `mgm`, `co_occurrence`, `wtna_cooccurrence`) describe
which actions or variables go together (Saqr, Beck, & López-Pernas,
2024). `frequency` keeps the counts of the transitions instead of their
probabilities, and `co_occurrence` counts how often two actions occur in
the same sequence.

```{r}
frequency_net <- build_network(group_regulation_long, action = "Action",
                               actor = "Actor", time = "Time",
                               method = "frequency")
splot(frequency_net)
```

```{r}
co_occurrence_net <- build_network(group_regulation_long, action = "Action",
                                   actor = "Actor", time = "Time",
                                   method = "co_occurrence")
splot(co_occurrence_net, layout = "spring")
```

# Stability of the edges

An edge estimated from one sample may not hold in another.
`bootstrap_network()` resamples the sequences with replacement, re-estimates
the network in each resample and reports, for each edge, its mean, its 95%
interval and a p-value (Saqr et al., 2025). By default the p-value is the
share of resamples in which the edge's weight falls outside a consistency
range of 0.75 to 1.25 times its original weight, so an edge with a small
p-value keeps its size across resamples.

```{r}
set.seed(265)
boot <- bootstrap_network(net, iter = 1000)
boot
```

Of the 78 edges, 51 are stable at the 5% level. The strongest transitions
are also the most precise: `cohesion` to `consensus` has a mean of 0.50
and an interval of [0.47, 0.52].

`splot()` draws the stable edges solid and the others dashed; `display =
"significant"` draws only the stable edges, `display = "full"` all edges
alike, and `show_stars = TRUE` or `show_ci = TRUE` add the significance
stars or the intervals to the edge labels.

```{r}
splot(boot)
```

```{r}
splot(boot, display = "significant")
```

```{r}
splot(boot, show_ci = TRUE)
```

A forest plot shows the estimate and the interval of every edge; `layout`
arranges the edges in a list, a circle or groups.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 14
plot_bootstrap_forest(boot, show_ci = TRUE)
```

# Stability of the centralities

Centrality measures summarise each node's position in the network.
`centrality_stability()` drops increasing proportions of the sequences,
recomputes the centralities, and correlates them with the centralities of
the full data (Epskamp, Borsboom, & Fried, 2018). The CS-coefficient is the
largest proportion of sequences that can be dropped while the correlation
stays above 0.7 in 95% of the resamples; Epskamp et al. (2018) treat values
above 0.5 as acceptable.

```{r}
set.seed(265)
cs <- centrality_stability(net, iter = 500)
cs
splot(cs)
```

The CS-coefficients of in-strength, out-strength and betweenness are all
0.90: the ranking of the actions by these measures holds when 90% of the
sequences are removed.

# Group networks

`group =` estimates one network per value of a covariate and returns a
group of networks (López-Pernas, Tikka, & Saqr, 2025). `splot()` draws the
groups side by side on a common scale, so edge widths can be compared
across panels.

```{r}
group_net <- build_network(group_regulation_long, action = "Action",
                           actor = "Actor", time = "Time",
                           method = "relative", group = "Achiever")
group_net
splot(group_net)
```

`bootstrap_network()` on the group resamples each group.

```{r}
set.seed(265)
group_boot <- bootstrap_network(group_net, iter = 500)
splot(group_boot)
```

# Comparing groups

`permutation()` compares the networks of the groups edge by edge: it
shuffles the group labels of the sequences, recomputes the difference of
every edge, and compares the observed difference with the shuffled ones
(Saqr et al., 2025). On a group of networks it compares every pair of
groups.

```{r}
set.seed(265)
group_perm <- permutation(group_net, iter = 1000)
group_perm
```

The networks of high and low achievers differ: 42 of the 78 transitions
differ at the 5% level, and the global statistic M, the sum of the
absolute edge differences, is 2.61 (p = 0.001).

```{r}
head(summary(group_perm), 10)
```

`weight_x` and `weight_y` are the transition probabilities of high and
low achievers, `diff` their difference, and `effect_size` the difference
in standard deviations of the permuted differences. For example, low
achievers move from `cohesion` to `coregulate` more often (0.17 against
0.08), and high achievers from `cohesion` to `consensus` (0.54 against
0.45).

`splot()` draws the edges that differ, coloured by the group in which they
are stronger.

```{r}
splot(group_perm, edge_positive_color = "#4A6FE3",
      edge_negative_color = "#D33F6A")
```

Blue edges are stronger among high achievers and red edges among low
achievers; `show_nonsig = TRUE` adds the edges that do not differ, and
`show_stars = TRUE` the significance stars.

# Clusters of states

The nine actions fall into two groups of behaviour: regulation of the task
(`monitor`, `plan`, `coregulate`, `adapt`) and social interaction
(`cohesion`, `consensus`, `discuss`, `emotion`, `synthesis`).
`build_mcml()` estimates a multi-cluster, multi-level network: a network of
the clusters, and a network of the actions within each cluster (Zhang et
al., 2026).

```{r}
clusters <- list(
  Regulatory = c("monitor", "plan", "coregulate", "adapt"),
  Social     = c("cohesion", "consensus", "discuss", "emotion", "synthesis")
)
cluster_net <- build_mcml(net, clusters = clusters)
cluster_net
splot(cluster_net)
```

At the level of the clusters, both kinds of action are followed more often
by a social action: a regulatory action by a social one with probability
0.60, and a social action by another social action with probability 0.61.
`as_tna()` converts the levels into transition networks, one for the
clusters and one for the actions within each cluster.

```{r}
cluster_levels <- as_tna(cluster_net)
splot(cluster_levels)
```
